text:
Recent work separates recurring intent from immediate demand. [HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/) combines latent intent clustering, Hawkes processes for recurring interests, and attention for short-term adaptation. [TSRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08531) models user-specific repeat intervals, item-specific intervals, and similarity to previous repeat sequences. These support learning when interests recur, but do not establish that an interaction leaves a need unsatisfied. [TALE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07382) offers a cheaper starting point: temporal weighting of item transitions and normalization for changing popularity.

Complementarity and substitution depend on context: controlled experiments found interactions between recommendation type and purchase decision stage, challenging a single similarity-based relevance score. This evidence predates the requested period and does not identify satisfaction from interaction logs. ([Zhang and Bockstedt, 2020](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378720620302792)) Practical hypothesis for this benchmark: augment SASRec with a small elapsed-time-conditioned gate over persistent preference, recent intent, and directed item transitions; optionally test temporary suppression of close semantic neighbors after an interaction, with learned recovery over time. Titles/descriptions can supply text similarity without pretrained weights; training histories supply transition evidence. Treat these as predictive proxies, never observed complement/substitute or satisfaction labels. Because simulator recommendations exclude seen items, exact-item repeat models need adaptation to recurring semantic interests. Use only timestamps available at prediction; if query time is absent, avoid target-time leakage. Select through the fixed four-category macro validation HR@10.
